passage:
At the Diwali gathering, Alka Masi pressed a red envelope into Shalini's hand. "For you, gudiya." Shalini's eyes went round. She wanted a doll as big as a house.
Mummy held out her hand. "Give it to me for safekeeping."
"But it's mine!"
"It's yours because Masi loves you. We'll keep it safe and write who gave it, so you can say thank you. You can choose one small thing."
Shalini held it a moment, then handed it over. "A small doll."
"A small doll," Mummy agreed.

qa.q: What colour was the envelope Alka Masi gave Shalini?
qa.a: The envelope was red.

qa.q: What was Shalini feeling when she first held the envelope?
qa.a: She felt excited, and her eyes went round because she wanted a doll as big as a house.

qa.q: What did Shalini choose to do after Mummy explained, and what did that show?
qa.a: She handed over the envelope and asked for a small doll, which shows she began to see the money as tied to Masi's love and to family rules.

qa.q: Why might Mummy write down who gave the gift?
qa.a: Mummy may want Shalini to remember to say thank you and to see the gift as part of a relationship, not just money to spend.

grounding: A child receives a cash envelope at a festival and hands it to a parent, learning that money is tied to relationships and family rules.

"Papa, look! Siddharth Uncle gave me kaineettam!" said Chetan on Vishu morning, waving a white envelope.
"Lovely. What do you say?"
"Thank you, Uncle!"
"Now give it to me and I'll put it in the puja cupboard."
"Why? It's mine!"
"It's yours, and it's also a blessing. In our house we keep it safe, and when you want something small, we talk about it."
Chetan frowned. "Can I look first?" He peeked at the note, then placed the envelope in Papa's hand.

qa.q: What did Chetan receive from Siddharth Uncle on Vishu morning?
qa.a: Chetan received kaineettam in a white envelope.

qa.q: What was Chetan feeling when he asked 'Why? It's mine!'?
qa.a: He felt possessive and a little upset at losing the envelope he had just received.

qa.q: What did Chetan choose to do after Papa explained, and what did it show?
qa.a: He looked at the note once more and then placed the envelope in Papa's hand, showing he was accepting that this money belongs to a blessing and family rules.

qa.q: How might Siddharth Uncle have felt seeing Chetan wave the envelope happily?
qa.a: He probably felt pleased that Chetan was so glad of the blessing, although the passage does not say what he thought.

grounding: A child receives cash in an envelope at a festival and hands it to a parent, learning money is tied to relationships and family rules.

passage:
At his cousin's wedding, Siddharth, five, touched the elders' feet. A tall uncle slipped a white envelope into his hand. "Shagun, beta."
A note! He could buy the biggest balloon.
But Mumma, Sarita, held out her hand. "Give it to me, Siddharth. We'll keep it safe."
His lip trembled. "But he gave it to ME."
Mumma knelt. "He gave it with love. We'll write his name in our book and give back at his grandson's birthday."
Siddharth handed it over slowly. Mumma gave him a coin. "For the balloon." He ran.

qa.q: What did the tall uncle slip into Siddharth's hand?
qa.a: He slipped a white envelope into his hand, saying "Shagun, beta."

qa.q: What was Siddharth feeling when his lip trembled?
qa.a: Siddharth felt disappointed and upset, since he thought the money was his to spend.

qa.q: How did Mumma help Siddharth understand?
qa.a: She explained simply that the gift shows love and that the family gives back, and she gave him a coin for the balloon.

qa.q: How might the tall uncle see giving shagun?
qa.a: He sees it as a way to show love and blessing to a child in the family.

grounding: A child receives shagun at a wedding and is told to hand it to his mother, learning that money is tied to relationships and family rules.

"Kalyani, what's in your hand?"
"Bua gave me an envelope for Bhai Dooj! Look, Mamma, money!"
"How lovely. Now give it to me."
"Why? It's mine."
"Because you're five, and envelopes go in the family box. When Bua's children come, we give them envelopes too."
"So it's not my money?"
Jaya laughed. "It's family money with your name on it. What did you want to buy?"
"A pink hair clip."
"Then we'll buy one tomorrow, from the box. Deal?"
Kalyani thought hard. "Deal. But I want to put it in the box myself."

qa.q: What did Kalyani want to buy?
qa.a: Kalyani wanted a pink hair clip.

qa.q: How did Kalyani feel when she was asked to hand the envelope over?
qa.a: She felt confused and a bit upset, thinking the money was hers.

qa.q: What did Jaya do that helped Kalyani accept the rule?
qa.a: Jaya explained simply that envelopes go in the family box because the family gives back, and offered to buy the clip.

qa.q: How might Bua feel about Kalyani's reaction?
qa.a: Bua would probably be amused and pleased that Kalyani was so excited by her gift.

grounding: A child receives a festival envelope and is told to hand it to her mother, learning that money is tied to family relationships and rules.

passage:
Kindergarten teacher's note, after Raksha Bandhan.
In sharing circle, Naveen, five, said his cousins gave him envelopes with money at Raksha Bandhan. "But Mummy took them," he said, frowning. "She says it's for giving back."
One child said her grandmother lets her keep hers. Naveen looked upset.
I told the circle that every family has its own rules about gifts, and that money given at festivals is often a way of saying "we love you."
At pickup, his mother, Devika, said she keeps a notebook of every gift and returns it at others' festivals.
Next step: drawing "gifts in my family."

qa.q: What did Naveen say his mummy says about the envelopes?
qa.a: She says it's for giving back.

qa.q: What was Naveen feeling when he frowned?
qa.a: Naveen felt disappointed and a bit confused that the money was taken away.

qa.q: What did the teacher say that helped the children?
qa.a: The teacher explained that every family has its own rules about gifts and that festival money is often a way of saying "we love you."

qa.q: How does Devika seem to see festival gifts?
qa.a: Devika sees them as part of a relationship to be returned, which is why she keeps a notebook.

grounding: A teacher's note shows a child who receives festival money and hands it to his mother, learning that money is tied to relationships and family rules.

passage: At the wedding in Bathinda, Nandini Bua bent down and gave Hrithik a red envelope with a gold border. "Shagun, for my big boy!" Hrithik felt the crinkle inside. He wanted a toy truck from the fair. "Give it to Mummy, beta," Papa said. Hrithik's lip wobbled. He handed it over slowly. Mummy knelt down. "This is from Bua because she loves you. We'll keep it safe, and at the fair you can choose one thing." Hrithik ran back to Bua and hugged her legs.

qa.q: What colour was the envelope?
qa.a: It was a red envelope with a gold border.

qa.q: What was Hrithik feeling when Papa told him to give the envelope to Mummy?
qa.a: He felt disappointed, and his lip wobbled, because he had hoped to buy a toy truck.

qa.q: What did Mummy say that helped Hrithik understand?
qa.a: She explained the money came from Bua's love, that it would be kept safe, and that he could still choose one thing at the fair.

qa.q: How might Nandini Bua feel when Hrithik hugs her legs?
qa.a: Bua probably feels happy and loved, seeing that he understands the gift came from her.
